@coll09 draws a relational comparison between knowledge and power. The point is that knowledge will enable an individual to obtain what they want out of life. She then argues that historically, knowledge in marginalized communities has been suppressed. What Collins means by suppression of knowledge, however, occurs through the suppression of the intellectual contribution of black women in broader American society. Of course, her concern can be extended to include any individual whose intellectual contribution to the epistemic landscape of the community they reside in has been suppressed.

Namely, the intellectual views of marginalized groups on poverty, oppression, independence etc. However, these knowledge domains, largely influential in formal education, are not central to more important knowledge domains. It is these other knowledge domains that are central to the flourishing of a culture and an individual. The source of these other knowledge domains is first in the home, for it is in the home where we learn who we are, what matters to us, and most importantly, that we are loved and desired. In other words, the source for this other second-personal knowledge exists within the contexts of special relationships.
